records.name: Western Visayas
records.summary:
On 10 October 2022 the Capiz State University Office of Student Affairs told students perceived as trans women that they would be barred from university premises unless they cut their hair and wore the uniform prescribed for males, delivering the instruction through campus guards with one week to comply and threatening that they could not re-enroll otherwise; the office attributed the order to the university president. A legal-NGO case study documents the students' subsequent advocacy campaign — backed by paralegals of national LGBTQ organisations, who pointed to an existing municipal anti-discrimination ordinance in Roxas City, Capiz, which the office dismissed as inapplicable — and its later milestone: the first openly trans woman graduating as university valedictorian with highest honours. This is a documented episode of institutional gender-expression policing in a provincial (not metropolitan) setting, reversed by advocacy.

No killings from the 2024-2025 national series occurred in this region. The campus directive is a resident-facing action rather than a mechanism a visitor encounters; its force as a region signal is that in a conservative provincial setting expression can be policed by institutional authority without an operational local recourse — unlike Central Visayas, this region has no protective ordinance cluster of comparable reach.

records.name: Ilocos Region
records.summary:
The Pangasinan provincial board certified and affirmed Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023 of Bayambang protecting the rights of LGBTQI persons (Provincial Board Resolution No. 799-2024, session of 19 August 2024)—a provincial-level endorsement of a municipal LGBTQ+ protection ordinance in a conservative province. This gives a visitor in the Pangasinan corridor a local complaint route absent in most other regions.

Against that, the Abra and Ilocos Sur provinces within Ilocos Region host the Bodong Indigenous Allied Group (BIAG), a codified customary-justice system with its own dispute-resolution authority over "crimes and tribal-related offences," recognised by Philippine courts. No trans-specific bodong ruling or customary exclusion was documented, but the legal-pluralism structure means that in a rural Abra or Ilocos Sur dispute, the applicable institution may not be a Philippine court.

Net effect: +0.03 above the national score, modest because the protective ordinance is municipal and the plural-justice uncertainty is localized to specific provinces within the region. Compare Central Visayas (0.63), where the ordinance cluster is broader (city IRRs with UNDP backing, unanimous municipal votes) and there is no countervailing alternative-justice structure.

records.name: ARMM
records.summary:
In the Bangsamoro autonomous region justice is legally plural: the region's 2019 administrative code provides that it be dispensed in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, and traditional or tribal laws (the clause is carried in the research dossier; the cached code excerpt does not reach it), while the national Code of Muslim Personal Laws of 1977 remains in force. In July 2026 the Bangsamoro parliament tabled a bill for a comprehensive Shari'ah justice system code extending to ta'zir criminal offences — the category under which morality offences are prosecuted in comparable systems. No source establishes that Philippine Shari'ah courts currently prosecute same-sex conduct or gender expression, and no such law has yet passed.

The Shari'ah court system is expanding nationally: three new judicial districts and twelve circuit courts beyond BARMM were created by law signed in August 2024, extending into majority-Christian areas, with further access legislation in September 2025 and a Supreme Court resolution in January 2026 to operationalise the Shari'ah High Court.

The finding for a trans visitor is structural rather than enforcement-based: a dispute could fall outside the civil courts altogether, in a jurisdiction actively legislating criminal religious law with no protective ordinance or civil-rights infrastructure documented in the region. Forward-looking, and bounded by the fact that the ta'zir code is a proposal, not a power in force.

records.name: CAR
records.summary:
In the Cordillera administrative region, inter-tribal customary justice runs alongside the formal system: the Kalinga bodong/pagta peace-pact system — with its own holders, sanctions and authority over crimes and tribal-related offences — was codified in February 2026 by the provincial government into a 137-page written Pagta, a step its sponsors present as recognition by the national courts. Academic documentation frames this as legal pluralism in which customary resolution of criminal and tribal offences operates with police, prosecutors and local officials participating, and constitutional recognition of indigenous justice extends across the country's autonomous regions.

No trans-specific bodong ruling, customary exclusion or punishment relating to gender expression appears in this record. The finding for a visitor is structural uncertainty — which forum decides a dispute — without any evidence of a trans-specific adverse outcome: the customary system here is a civil and restorative-justice institution with no criminal-law expansion over morality documented, which keeps it a marginal concern, not a threat finding.

records.name: Daegu
records.summary:
Daegu has hosted the country's second-oldest queer culture festival every year since June 2009 — organisers mark seventeen consecutive years 'without fail', run 'as a form of resistance against hate and discriminatory politics', the 2025 edition under the slogan 'We Will Not Be E(r)ased' on central Daegu's Dongseong-ro. Organisers cite a Supreme Court ruling on local anti-discrimination ordinances as confirming sexual minorities as citizens protected by the Constitution.

The festival draws a recurring, organised counter-mobilisation: in September 2025 a Daegu–Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer', gathering roughly 3,500 believers from some 1,600 churches from Banwoldang station along a 450-metre stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans, timed against the festival. For a visible trans visitor the result is a concentrated confrontational environment during festival week; the event itself continues to take place annually despite interference.

records.name: Daejeon
records.summary:
In October 2021 the Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the Army's forced discharge of transgender soldier Byun Hee-soo, holding the military should have considered her a woman when reviewing fitness for duty — a ruling widely described as a landmark in the case brought to repeal the discharge decision.

On 24 June 2024, after the Ministry of National Defense reversed the Army's original 'natural death' classification and recognised the 2021 death as service-related, Byun was interred at the National Cemetery in Daejeon. Around 60 activists gathered to protest the burial, arguing her service did not qualify her for interment there: state recognition of a trans person at the national memorial ground, met with a small but public rejection in open space.

records.name: North Chungcheong
records.summary:
North Chungcheong (capital: Cheongju) is scored −0.02 below the national 0.71 on the basis of the Byun Hee-soo case and its institutional aftermath, with the single-incident caveat applied explicitly. Byun, 23, was found dead in her Cheongju home on 3 March 2021 (apparent suicide) following forced military discharge and during ongoing mental-health counselling at a centre near her residence. Initial police and Army handling classified the death as 'natural'; this was overturned only three years later (April 2024) when the Ministry of National Defense's Central Military Casualty Review Board recognised it as service-related. The wrongful initial classification is the evidence: it reflects an institutional denial of the connection between anti-trans policy and a trans person's death, corrected only after sustained advocacy.

Per the single-incident rule, one death cannot establish a Cheongju pattern, and no repeat violence data exists for this unit. It is included at −0.02 rather than zero because Chungcheongbuk-do is small enough for one nationally prominent case to carry weight, and because the institutional response (wrongful classification sustained for three years before correction) is a state-implicated finding. Compared to Daejeon (0.69), which hosts the positive court ruling that corrected the same institution's error, North Chungcheong's share of the Byun story is purely negative—but the deviation is identical because the correction (Daejeon court, MND board) already mitigates the initial harm.

records.name: South Chungcheong
records.summary:
South Chungcheong (Chungcheongnam-do) was swept into the same provincial fight over student human-rights protections that engulfed Seoul, but with the institutions on opposite sides: on 24 April 2024 the provincial council passed a bill to repeal the Chungcheongnam-do Student Human Rights Ordinance (in force since 10 July 2020; its Article 15 stipulates non-discrimination obligations based on gender identity and sexual orientation), and the provincial Office of Education sued to overturn it, obtaining a suspension of the repeal's execution from the Supreme Court on 30 May 2024, so the ordinance remains in effect. On 21 February 2025 the Chungcheongnam-do and Seoul offices of education filed a joint response to a communication from three UN special procedures, appearing as 'stakeholders (enforcing authorities)' in the repeal dispute still pending before the Supreme Court and opposing the rollback on constitutional and treaty grounds.

The evidence is primarily resident-facing (student non-discrimination rules), carrying small weight for a traveler under the scoring rules; no traveler-facing enforcement action, arrest, or event obstruction is documented for this unit.
